final_proof:
The claim is false under the stated assumption that \(f\) is merely integrable. The correct result requires additional smoothness; for example, it holds when \(f\in C^2([a,b])\). We first give a counterexample and then prove the corrected theorem.

Assume \(a<b\) and \(n\geq1\), and write
\[
h=\frac{b-a}{n},\qquad x_r=a+rh,
\]
and
\[
T_n(f)=\frac h2\left(f(x_0)+f(x_n)+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}f(x_r)\right).
\]

For the failure of the statement as written, take \(a=0\), \(b=1\), \(n=1\), and
\[
f(x)=\left|x-\frac12\right|.
\]
This function is continuous, hence integrable, and
\[
\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=\frac14,
\qquad
T_1(f)=\frac12\bigl(f(0)+f(1)\bigr)=\frac12.
\]
Thus the magnitude of the error is \(1/4\). On the other hand, \(f''(x)=0\) for every \(x\ne1/2\), while \(f''(1/2)\) does not exist. Consequently there is no \(\xi\in[0,1]\) for which the proposed expression \(f''(\xi)/12\) equals the nonzero error. Hence integrability alone does not imply the claimed error formula.

Here is the standard corrected statement. If \(f\in C^2([a,b])\), then there exists \(\xi\in[a,b]\) such that
\[
T_n(f)-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
=\frac{(b-a)^3}{12n^2}f''(\xi). \tag{2}
\]
Equivalently, if error is defined as exact value minus approximation, then
\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-T_n(f)
=-\frac{(b-a)^3}{12n^2}f''(\xi). \tag{3}
\]

To prove this, fix \(r\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), put \(u=x_{r-1}\), \(v=x_r\), and define
\[
w(x)=(x-u)(v-x)\quad (u\leq x\leq v).
\]
Then \(w(u)=w(v)=0\), \(w'(u)=h\), \(w'(v)=-h\), and \(w''=-2\). Two integrations by parts give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_u^v w(x)f''(x)\,dx
&=-\int_u^v w'(x)f'(x)\,dx\\
&=-[w'(x)f(x)]_u^v+\int_u^v w''(x)f(x)\,dx\\
&=h\bigl(f(u)+f(v)\bigr)-2\int_u^v f(x)\,dx.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that the local trapezium error is
\[
\frac h2\bigl(f(u)+f(v)\bigr)-\int_u^v f(x)\,dx
=\frac12\int_u^v(x-u)(v-x)f''(x)\,dx. \tag{4}
\]
Summing (4) over all subintervals yields
\[
T_n(f)-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
=\frac12\sum_{r=1}^n\int_{x_{r-1}}^{x_r}
(x-x_{r-1})(x_r-x)f''(x)\,dx. \tag{5}
\]

The piecewise-defined weight in (5) is nonnegative and has positive total integral. Since \(f''\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), the weighted mean-value theorem for integrals therefore supplies some \(\xi\in[a,b]\) for which the right-hand side of (5) equals
\[
\frac12f''(\xi)\sum_{r=1}^n\int_{x_{r-1}}^{x_r}
(x-x_{r-1})(x_r-x)\,dx.
\]
On each subinterval, substituting \(t=x-x_{r-1}\) gives
\[
\int_{x_{r-1}}^{x_r}(x-x_{r-1})(x_r-x)\,dx
=\int_0^h t(h-t)\,dt=\frac{h^3}{6}.
\]
Consequently
\[
T_n(f)-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
=\frac12f''(\xi)n\frac{h^3}{6}
=\frac{nh^3}{12}f''(\xi)
=\frac{(b-a)^3}{12n^2}f''(\xi),
\]
because \(h=(b-a)/n\). This proves (2), and negating both sides proves (3).

As an independent check on the sign, take \(f(x)=x^2\), \([a,b]=[0,1]\), and \(n=1\). Then \(T_1(f)=1/2\), \(\int_0^1f=1/3\), and \(f''=2\). Thus
\[
T_1(f)-\int_0^1f=\frac16=\frac1{12}\,f'',
\]
confirming that the displayed positive expression is approximation minus exact value; the opposite error convention has the minus sign.
